results.input: To which German spa did the Cantankerous Old Lady need to travel?
results.reply: Schlangenbad, dear — that was the place, and Lady Georgina engaged me as her maid to get there. A week's wages and a temper to match the German weather; I've seldom had a stranger introduction to a watering-place.

results.input: On the train from Ostend, at which station did the Count fear you might have to give up your compartment?
results.reply: At Brussels — the Count made a great show of fearing the train was so crowded that I must give up my place, and Lady Georgina would have none of it. He was trying to get me out of the carriage, of course, and I fancy I guessed as much even then.

results.reply: Cyrus W. Hitchcock, of Hitchcock, Hitchcock and Co. He turned up at Frankfort hard on my heels, licenses and all, and proposed the Great Manitou and a race to Limburg. He also proposed something else, which I declined with thanks.

results.input: What did you remember, from the college laboratory, that a blackish film like the one on the bangle might be?
results.reply: Sulphur, of course — I had it from Girton, where I once blackened a silver spoon in the laboratory and never forgot the smell of it. Silver tarnishes to that film at the least touch of sulphur, so I had only to press the bangle against a rubber bottle and watch the miracle turn common chemistry. Poor Mrs. Evelegh, to have her soul weighed by a bit of chemistry she had never been taught.

results.input: When you climbed up the rope to the top, how many nooses did you know there were?
results.reply: Nooses! You make it sound like Tyburn. As I went over the edge I had one loop under my arms and one knotted at the plaid's corners — and the third I tied only when I reached Harold, since it was his weight, not mine, that mattered. Elsie above counted every knot with me, I promise you, and none of the three was meant for a neck.

results.input: In Florence, who did you recognise the urbane old gentleman to be?
results.reply: Mr. Ashurst, dear — Marmaduke Ashurst himself, Harold's uncle, though he came into our little typewriting office as a stranger wanting stock-exchange letters. I confess I guessed him sooner than he guessed me.

results.input: In the oasis, where had the veiled Englishwoman first been sold to a man?
results.reply: She told me she had been taken at Khartoum and first sold to a man in the slave market at Omdurman, poor soul. After that she was bought and carried off to Wadi Bou, wife to the chief there.

results.reply: Lord Southminster, on the Jumna, no less — he had the impudence to tell me he had come aboard to superintend the preparations for my reception in India. Which meant, when one translated his lordship's English, that he had come to spy on me and to make sure Mr Ashurst's money should find its way into his own pocket. I told him plainly what I thought of such a commission.

results.reply: In our own office in Florence, sir — the little typewriting establishment Elsie and I had set up there. Mr Ashurst came to us, dictated his stock-exchange letters and then his will, and I copied it out with my own ten fingers. Which is precisely how I knew, when they showed me the impounded document, that the thing was a forgery — my x never broke, and I never made those errors.

results.reply: The make? I don't think I ever swore to a make of machine, and I shouldn't pretend otherwise. What betrayed that document was the typing itself: blunders I would never have made, and a broken x that stamped it as Higginson's copy of the rough draft rather than my clean work. The brand of the thing was the least of it; the letters were the confession.

results.input: What name was on the card the foreign gentleman handed to Lady Georgina?
results.reply: A French card, all flourishes — the Count de Laroche, as he styled himself, with the waxed moustache to match. The same gentleman, you may be sure, who was so very anxious to relieve Lady Georgina of her jewel-case at Malines.

results.reply: He hemmed and hawed scandalously — a military bicycle race was no place for a young woman, he said — but when it came to the regulations he could find nothing to forbid me, so he shrugged and let me enter. I fancy he was rather pleased to see me win, though he'd never have admitted it.

results.reply: A Russian novel, of all absurd things — Tolstoi, I fancy; the Austrian officials seemed to think a book could corrupt an empire, and my trunks sat in bond while they satisfied themselves I was not an anarchist in petticoats.

results.reply: Bombay — we took the P. and O. steamer from Suez, Elsie and I, and Higginson turned up on board as Southminster's courier, which was the first sour note of the voyage.

results.reply: A rifle, and I said so plainly to the Maharajah — I had never held one in my life, nor wished to. Which made the business with the tiger and my elephant all the more ridiculous, as you may imagine.

results.reply: She never put it to me so plainly as all that — only that her brother-in-law had made it in the City, and that she would not hear it called trade. Money, in her mouth, was always a thing to be mentioned and never explained.

results.reply: The cross-eyed Queen's Counsel who had baited me in the witness-box. He came to apologise for his conduct, and then had the impudence to propose marriage—the most uncomfortable compliment I ever received.

results.reply: Behind the little drawer at the back of the desk, where the slope of the top hides it — the rest of the thing was pigeon-holes and a mystery. I found the spring by tapping, and Mr. Hayes and I broke the panel open together; the genuine will had been lying there all along while Higginson's copy did its mischief in the courts.

results.reply: She tore it up, with a snort of contempt — she had never before met a woman who refused money, and she didn't quite know whether to be vexed or impressed. I fancy the refusal did me more good with her than the twenty guineas would have done.

results.reply: Precious little, I can tell you — the ragged remnant of my own savings, a sovereign or two and a handful of silver. Enough to carry me to Frankfort and a cheap pension, and not a penny more. Which is precisely why I would not take Lady Georgina's loan.

results.reply: Twenty-five percent on every machine I sent his way. He grumbled a little, as Americans do when a woman names a figure first, but he agreed — and it has kept me in railway tickets ever since.

results.input: What price did you give them for it?
results.reply: Twenty pounds apiece, and Cyrus allowed me a commission on the two. I told them it would climb hills like a goat and be worth every sovereign.

results.reply: Nailed boots, dear, the kind one wears for climbing. They bit into the turf and left a clear little pattern of spikes on the softer ground above the screes, which was how I knew he had gone that way and not down the valley path. A good thing too, for the marks stopped at the edge of a slope, and below it the hawks were circling.

results.reply: As like one another as the beads on a string: a mud bank, a cluster of flat-roofed hovels, a minaret, three palms and a crowd of donkeys. After the second you might as well have saved your eyes and slept through the rest of the river.

results.reply: From his own uncle, Mr. Marmaduke Ashurst. Higginson had been Mr. Ashurst's courier before that, and Southminster knew perfectly well he was a rogue when he took him on.

results.reply: I pulled the trigger, if that's what you mean, but I will not pretend it was a clean shot aimed by a heroine. The brute was clawing at my elephant, Southminster was bungling, the Maharajah shouted at him to hold his fire, and my rifle went off in the general scrimmage. It killed the tiger; the natives cut off the whiskers before anyone could see where the bullet had entered, so I was toasted as a shikari and could not very well contradict them.

results.input: At what time was the detective due in Edinburgh, so that you had to marry before?
results.reply: I could not have named you the minute to swear to it in a court of law, but I know it was a race against the clock: the detective's warrant for the handcuffs was timed to Edinburgh, and we had only the quarter of an hour at Dunbar to be married and be properly Mr and Mrs before the train ran on. That was the whole crux, you see. The man sat in the very next carriage watching us through the glass, and Harold judged it better to be married and then surrender than to let a policeman's convenience decide when I should be a wife.

results.reply: Higginson forged it, the wretch, and Southminster put it forward and swore to it as though it were gospel. White only hid it in the desk and held his tongue.

results.input: I mean her sharp hints at Schlangenbad: what sort of women did she go on about?
results.reply: Adventuresses, always — the penniless sort with a good accent and a bad conscience, who angle for a rich husband and bring a family to ruin. She warned me against them with such relish that I nearly took notes, and only later did I learn she had brought me there precisely so her Harold would fall in love with a portionless girl and give his relatives a quarrel to chew on. I have never been so handsomely insulted in my life, nor so usefully.

results.reply: I told him his aunt ought to have been there as a proper chaperon, though between ourselves I would have chosen almost anyone else in Europe for the post. Lady Georgina as a guardian of propriety is rather like setting a fox to mind the hen-house. And I fancy Harold was heartily glad she was safely at Schlangenbad.

results.reply: As his sister's maid, dear — that was the tale he told me, never dreaming the maid was the woman at his own typewriter. He said Georgina had picked up a young person in Kensington Gardens to attend her to Schlangenbad, and that this same young person had saved the jewel-case from the Count. I let him finish the story before I owned that the young person was I.

results.reply: On Harold, of course. He told me Harold would get nothing, that the will was as good as dead, and that I was staking my all on a losing horse when I might have a coronet instead. As if love were a wager at Ascot and I a bookmaker's clerk. I told him I loved Harold and would marry him if he hadn't a penny to his name, and sent him about his business.

results.input: I mean when you tried to explain your engagement: on what condition had you said you would marry Harold?
results.reply: That I had promised to marry Harold only when he was poor and friendless. The cross-eyed gentleman made it sound like the most mercenary vow ever uttered by woman, as if poverty were a dowry I was scheming for. I dare say it did look absurd in a court of law, but I meant it, and I would say it again.
